group.title: Technology and innovation
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A new idea, method or product.
examples: The phone was full of clever {innovations}.
wrong: The innovation was the same old idea that everyone already used.

words.meaning: Using new and original ideas.
examples: The company is known for its {innovative} designs.
wrong: The design was innovative, so it copied an old model exactly.

words.meaning: An important new discovery or development.
examples: Scientists made a {breakthrough} in battery design.
wrong: The breakthrough meant the research made no progress at all.

words.meaning: A small, useful tool or device.
examples: He loves kitchen {gadgets}, like his electric garlic peeler.
wrong: A gadget is a huge factory that builds ships.

words.meaning: A fast connection to the internet.
examples: We finally got {broadband}, so videos load instantly.
wrong: With broadband, it takes an hour to open one web page.

words.meaning: A website that helps you find information on the internet.
examples: Type the question into a {search engine}.
wrong: A search engine is the motor that makes a car go.

words.meaning: The use of machines and computers to do work instead of people.
examples: {Automation} has replaced many factory jobs.
wrong: Automation means every task is done by hand.

words.meaning: To make a process work by machines instead of people.
examples: The bank {automated} the payment process.
wrong: They automated the job, so now ten people do it by hand.

words.meaning: Computer images that make you feel as if you are in a real place.
examples: With a {virtual reality} headset, you can walk on the moon.
wrong: Virtual reality is the real world you see with your own eyes.

words.meaning: The newest and most advanced.
examples: The lab uses {cutting-edge} equipment.
wrong: The equipment was cutting-edge, so it was forty years old.

words.meaning: Using the most modern methods and materials.
examples: The hospital has a {state-of-the-art} scanner.
wrong: The gym is state-of-the-art, with broken machines from the 1970s.

words.meaning: Using the most advanced technology.
examples: The new office has a {high-tech} security system.
wrong: The kitchen is high-tech, with only a wood fire and a bucket.

words.meaning: A screen that you control by touching it with your finger.
examples: Tap the icon on the {touchscreen} to open the app.
wrong: A touchscreen only works when you use a mouse and keyboard.

words.meaning: The small mark on a screen that shows where you are typing or pointing.
examples: Move the {cursor} to the end of the line.
wrong: The cursor is the plug at the back of the computer.

words.meaning: To change information into a secret code so others cannot read it.
examples: The app {encrypts} all your messages.
wrong: They encrypted the file so anyone could read it easily.

words.meaning: A person who secretly gets into other people’s computer systems.
examples: A {hacker} stole thousands of passwords.
wrong: A hacker is someone who never uses a computer.

words.meaning: An attempt to damage or steal from a computer system.
examples: The bank’s website went down after a {cyberattack}.
wrong: A cyberattack is when a company protects its computers.

words.meaning: To make a copy of computer files in case the originals are lost.
examples: Always {back up} your photos before updating your phone.
wrong: I backed up my files, so I lost every one of them when the phone broke.

words.meaning: A small problem that stops something working properly.
examples: A {glitch} in the system delayed all the flights.
wrong: The glitch made the program work perfectly.

words.meaning: A mistake in a computer program that makes it work badly.
examples: The update fixes a {bug} that made the app close.
wrong: The bug made the program run faster and better.

words.meaning: Easy for people to use or understand.
examples: The new website is very {user-friendly}.
wrong: The app is so user-friendly that nobody can work out how to use it.

words.meaning: Able to work with another device or program.
examples: This charger isn’t {compatible} with my phone.
wrong: The printer is compatible with my laptop, so they can’t work together.

words.meaning: Old and no longer useful or modern.
examples: Our school computers are badly {outdated}.
wrong: The phone is outdated, so it is the newest model in the shop.

words.meaning: A person whose job is to look after or repair technical equipment.
examples: A {technician} came to fix our internet connection.
wrong: The technician has no idea how machines work.

words.meaning: To find and fix problems in a system or machine.
examples: I spent an hour {troubleshooting} the printer.
wrong: He troubleshot the problem by ignoring it completely.

words.meaning: A device that notices changes such as heat, light or movement.
examples: The lights turn on when the {sensor} detects movement.
wrong: The sensor can’t notice anything around it.

words.meaning: A small aircraft without a pilot, controlled from the ground.
examples: They filmed the wedding with a {drone}.
wrong: A drone is a large plane with a hundred passengers and two pilots.

words.meaning: Designed to be worn on the body.
examples: A fitness band is a popular {wearable} device.
wrong: A wearable gadget is one you must leave on your desk.

words.meaning: One of the tiny dots that make up an image on a screen.
examples: The photo is blurry because it has too few {pixels}.
wrong: A pixel is a huge picture that covers a whole wall.

words.meaning: The part of a computer that does the calculations and controls it.
examples: The laptop has a fast {processor}, so games run smoothly.
wrong: The processor is the bag you carry your laptop in.

words.meaning: Unwanted emails or messages, usually advertising, sent to many people.
examples: My inbox is full of {spam} about cheap watches.
wrong: Spam is the personal email your best friend sends you.

words.meaning: A way of making computers improve at tasks by learning from large amounts of data.
examples: The app uses {machine learning} to suggest songs you might like.
wrong: Machine learning means a computer can never change how it works.

words.meaning: Space on a device for keeping files and data.
examples: My phone has run out of {storage} for new photos.
wrong: With more storage, you can keep fewer files.

words.meaning: Knowing a lot about modern technology and how to use it.
examples: My {tech-savvy} niece set up my new phone in minutes.
wrong: He’s very tech-savvy, so he can’t turn on a computer.

words.meaning: A person who starts using a new product or technology as soon as it appears.
examples: As an {early adopter}, he bought the first model on launch day.
wrong: She’s an early adopter, so she waits ten years before buying anything new.

words.meaning: A person who designs or makes something new for the first time.
examples: The {inventor} of the telephone changed how people talk.
wrong: An inventor only copies things that other people made.

words.meaning: The science of designing and building robots.
examples: She is studying {robotics} at college.
wrong: Robotics is the study of old poems.

words.meaning: To turn a computer off and on again.
examples: If the screen freezes, try {rebooting} the computer.
wrong: He rebooted the laptop by leaving it on all night.

words.meaning: A legal right to be the only one who makes or sells an invention for a time.
examples: She applied for a {patent} on her new design.
wrong: With a patent, anyone can copy and sell your invention freely.

words.meaning: To suddenly stop working, said of a computer or program.
examples: My laptop {crashed} and I lost my work.
wrong: The program crashed, so it kept running smoothly all day.
